To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the binding of catechoamines at physiological concentrations by human serum and its constituent proteins has been investigated and the binding of catecolamines by albumin and very low density liproprotein has been characterized in some detail.
catecholamines are bound to human serum and serum proteins, and that the binding is rapid and not readily reversed by prolonged dialyses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the binding of catechoamines to proteins and the possible physiological consequences of the binding.
the binding of catechoamines to human serum and its constituent proteins.
the binding of catecolamines at physiological concentrations (10−8-10−10 mol/l) to human serum and its components.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the physiological role of the binding of adrenaline and noradrenaline to human serum and serum proteins is still unknown.

the binding of catechoamines is not only to albumin but also to other proteins and that the binding is rapid and irreversible and that the binding of noradrenaline is more than twice that of adrenaline.
catecholamines bind to human serum and to human serum proteins in vivo.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the binding of catecolamines to human serum is rapid, reversible, saturable, and that it is associated with a number of different serum proteins.

at concentrations of 100 pg (−)- noradrenaline/ml or 100 pg (±)- adrenaline/ml, 50 per cent or more of the catecholamine is bound to serum proteins and the major binding sites are on albumin, very low density and high density lipoproteins, IgM, α2-macrolglobulin and an unidentified protein of molecular weight about 200 000.

The main takeaway from our work is that
we can now use the binding of (−)-nor-adrenaline to albumin as a marker of albumin concentration in the blood.
catecholamines bind to proteins in the blood, which may affect their pharmacokinetics and their pharmacodynamic effects.
